The red lights is for adjusting, but the main reason red is used is because if the light is transmitted through a periscope inadvertently, it is harder to see at night both by the distance it travels and against the backdrop of the ocean.

Your zero bubble is correct. Its relatable to your "posture" under the ocean. Usually this is in regards to straightening the sub so you can target something properly. One way to think if this is if you are holding a gun and you are leaning back towards the sky, your shot will go over, and if you're hunched forward at a down angle your shot will go under the target. There are other reasons to zero bubble involving sonar as well.

Making depth 50 feet, is essentially preparing to surface. Before you surface you extend your periscope out so you can see what's above you or confirm your target. In the old days you had to do this because of technological limitations, nowadays this is not required.

Periscopes are all electronic now, and totally sealed, there is no longer a flood danger.
Yes, I should have been more clear. No worries, I love being wrong and learning new stuff.

Essentially a periscope is just two forty five degree mirrors reflecting like down a tube.

The mirrors go both ways and one concern back in the day was a small beam of light shining in the direction of ships pronounced "targets" we were aiming for. The obvious solution to this is to turn off the lights, but now you can't see anything.

So they did studies and red light was harder to see on the ocean, went less far, and easier to adjust on humans eyes.

Its worth mentioning surface ships also rig for red at night for the same reason. The difference is they have quite a few more holes for the light to escape through.

Periscope depth is classified. Probably can find strong hints at common ones on the internet but those exact numbers are actually classified. I'd say its a safe bet to interpret the 50 foot depth as "a prepatory step to surfacing".

Keep in mind, before a sub surfaces it needs to verify nothing is above it. There was actually a pretty public incident where a sub failed to properly check the water above it and when it surfaced it ran into a commercial fishing vessel.

More information can be found on that here: https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ehime_Maru_and_USS_Greeneville_collision
